title: Mitchell, Ronchi pleased with NZ's ability to dig into their reserve at the Basin
excerpt: Daryl Mitchell played out 258 balls with Glenn Phillips in a sixth-wicket partnership to force a draw
author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: New Zealand's escape in Wellington was put down by Daryl Mitchell to staying in the moment and repeating the same thing, ball after ball, for as long as it took. The hosts trailed by 352 after India made the highest Test total ever scored against New Zealand, and once a result was out of reach, their only job was to bat out time.

They did it over 120 overs and 557 minutes, with Mitchell and Glenn Phillips seeing off 43 overs together on the final day. New Zealand haven't had to do that often. The last time they batted and battled through to a draw was in Kanpur in 2021, when Rachin Ravindra and Ajaz Patel held on for the last wicket.

"I think just trying to be as present as you can," Mitchell said a day after the draw, "And watch the ball and try and repeat that for long periods of time. I guess the nature of this side is we play a lot of cricket with each other, so we know what makes each other tick as well. So, I mean, it's just being present, repeating it ball after ball after ball. It might be boring at times, but yeah, nice to get the job done.
"I love batting with a GP, across all three formats, it's seriously good fun and it was nice to do, I guess, a different style for both of us."

Neither Mitchell nor Phillips is a natural blocker, and it was their restraint that pleased batting coach Luke Ronchi most. "It's adaptability," he said. "You know your role and what you want to do in each moment. I think the way Rachin Ravindra goes about it, the way Daryl Mitchell goes about it, the way GP goes about it, it's all very different. But you also know that in those moments they're doing whatever's needed for the team and that's a pretty cool thing as well.

"The guys know how to bat long periods of time. It's making sure there's different things that were going through their minds. We chat to both of them [Mitchell and Phillips], there are times where they want to give it a whack and do something, have a bit of an ego about it, but to be able to pull that back and know that this is what's needed in the moment, I think it's fantastic.

"We haven't really been in a position like that before, especially in the time I've been involved. So I think, it's sort of, to take it forward into the next Test now and that in different situations we can adapt and make the most of those opportunities."
New Zealand also had help from the Basin Reserve surface, which got flatter and easier to bat on as the match went on. However, Mitchell expects the Hagley Oval in Christchurch to be livelier.

"The nature of the Basin surface is it usually starts pretty green," Mitchell said. "We probably didn't expect it to get that slow and low over the course of five days, but now we're here at Hagley and I'm sure there might be a bit of bounce in this one."

India took only three of the eight wickets they needed on the final day and shook hands shortly after the last hour began. Ronchi said the timing surprised him a little, but he understood the reasoning.

"Their bowlers had all bowled 50 overs [each in the match]. It's looking at the bigger picture of things and their fast bowlers have put in a lot of work. So each side has their ways of thinking about how you might try and get the result. So for them to do it the way they did, they felt that was the right way."
